newsitem.title: USA: Yawning trade gap seen shaving Q3 U.S. GDP growth.
newsitem.headline: Yawning trade gap seen shaving Q3 U.S. GDP growth.

text.p: A surprising drop in the volume of U.S. exports in July has analysts lowering their forecasts for overall economic growth in the third quarter.

A huge jump in the U.S. trade gap in July to $11.68 billion from a revised $8.19 billion in June will bolster forecasts for a third-quarter slowdown in gross domestic product (GDP) growth to the 2.0 to 2.5 percent area after a 4.8 percent reading in the second quarter, analysts said.
"It's another pretty clear sign of weakness going into the third quarter here," said Richard Koss at MFR Inc.

"Having exports going down like this at a time when we're already seeing declining retail sales gives credence to forecasts for GDP going back to 2.0 to 2.5 percent," said Koss, an international strategist at MFR.
Since GDP is calculated quarterly, with heavy emphasis placed on the first month of each quarter, July weakness takes on added significance, some said.

"These numbers dig a big hole for the third quarter," said Brian Jones, economist at Salomon Brothers. "Our GDP forecast was 1.75 percent before this report. Given the weakness in retail sales, you're not building much momentum."
Analysts struggled to explain a huge jump in the July trade shortfall with Western Europe, which ballooned to a record $4.245 billion from $761 million in June.
The European gap typically expands in July and since trade data are not seasonally adjusted, analysts expected a sharp pullback in August data.

"Don't draw any conclusions from the bilateral trade numbers, because they're not adjusted and we may get some payback next month," Jones said. "If you're going to be worried, be worried about the overall number. Clearly, the export numbers are very soft."

Exports fell 3.6 percent in July to $67.19 billion, while imports rose a more modest 1.2 percent to $78.87 billion, pushing the overall trade gap to its highest point since a monthly average at $12.9 billion in fourth-quarter 1987.

Yet analysts said the burgeoning gap would likely shrink in coming months. Most of the July import increase reflected higher oil prices, which should fade, while forward-looking indicators suggest exports will improve.
"I'm not alarmed by this report," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank. "Other data show export orders picking up and we knew (economic) growth was soft overseas."

Prolonged economic slumps in continental Europe and Japan, combined with weakness in Canada, the largest U.S. trading partner, should eventually give way to modest growth and revive flagging U.S. exports, analysts said.
Widespread efforts overseas to bolster growth via low official interest rates should eventually succeed, prompting greater demand for U.S. goods, they predicted.
"Looking around the world in industrialized countries with substantial monetary stimulus, that should revive growth in our trading partners," Berner said.
